[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This document describes the process for requesting, reviewing, recording, and closing exceptions to Golden Path conformance requirements, policy-as-code rules, and Verification Contract checks. It is the operational counterpart to the gate infrastructure described in PTN-INFRA-GOV-001 and the policy enforcement described in PTN-INFRA-GOV-002. Exception management is a prerequisite: the conformance gate and policy gates must not be set to fail-hard mode until this process is defined and published.
page_texts.4:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#who-this-is-for]

### Who This Is For

**Primary:** Product engineers and team leads whose pipelines have halted due to a conformance gate failure or policy evaluation violation and who need to know what to do next.

**Secondary:** Platform Engineering team members who triage exception tickets. Architects who review and approve exceptions.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#what-this-process-covers]

### What This Process Covers

- Exceptions to Golden Path structural requirements enforced by the Architecture Conformance Gate (PTN-INFRA-GOV-001)
- Exceptions to infrastructure policy rules enforced by the Policy-as-Code Enforcement gate (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002)
- Exceptions to Verification Contract checks triggered during fitness function evaluation (PTN-APP-GOV-001, PTN-GOV-AI-003)
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#what-this-process-does-not-cover]

### What This Process Does Not Cover

- Absolute prohibitions defined in the AI Governance Policy (PTN-GOV-AI-002) — those are hard-blocked with no exception path
- Changes to the Golden Path Catalog — those follow the catalog contribution and ARB review process documented in PTN-GOV-AI-001
- Escalation triggers in the AI Governance Policy — those pause the pipeline for human approval; they are not exceptions

page_texts.8:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#why-exceptions-exist]

### Why Exceptions Exist

No rule set can anticipate every legitimate engineering scenario. A Golden Path that is prescriptive enough to give consistent, compliance-defensible guidance will occasionally conflict with a genuine technical constraint that a specific team faces. The exception process is the pressure-release valve that prevents the governance system from becoming an obstacle to real work.

The exception process also functions as a feedback loop. When multiple teams file exceptions for the same rule, that is a signal that the rule or path needs refinement — not that teams should be penalized. Exception rates are tracked per path and reviewed quarterly specifically to identify those signals.

**PTN-GOV-AI-001** makes this explicit: *"If teams consistently deviate from a path, that is a signal the path needs updating — not that teams should be penalized."*
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#absolute-prohibitions-are-not-exceptions]

### Absolute Prohibitions Are Not Exceptions

The AI Governance Policy (PTN-GOV-AI-002) defines a category of **absolute prohibitions**: actions that are hard-blocked at the pipeline level with no override path. Examples include direct production deployment by an AI agent, AI agent access to secret stores, and AI agent modification of IAM policies. These cannot be excepted — the technical control blocks them regardless of any approval. If a team encounters an absolute prohibition, the correct path is to redesign the approach within the approved boundary, not to file an exception.

The four-part policy structure in PTN-GOV-AI-002 is: permitted use cases, absolute prohibitions, escalation triggers, and audit trail requirements. Only activities governed by policy rules (not absolute prohibitions) are eligible for exceptions.
page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#exception-rate-as-a-governance-signal]

### Exception Rate as a Governance Signal

Exception tickets are tracked in the catalog alongside adoption metrics. The target exception rate across all pipelines is **< 10%** (PTN-GOV-AI-001). When a specific path's exception rate exceeds this threshold at a quarterly review, Platform Engineering initiates a review of the rules generating exceptions — not a review of team compliance. High exception rates indicate the path is either too prescriptive for current engineering reality or that a common use case needs its own catalog variant.

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#exception-type-1-conformance-gate-failure-architecture-structure]

### Exception Type 1: Conformance Gate Failure (Architecture Structure)

**Trigger:** The Architecture Conformance Gate (PTN-INFRA-GOV-001) runs in fail-hard (`deny`) mode, finds a structural violation, and halts the pipeline. The Exception Router component automatically creates a triage ticket in the issue tracker with the full conformance report attached and notifies the on-call architect channel.

**You do not need to manually create a ticket.** The Exception Router creates it when the gate fails.

**Common causes:** Missing required directory structure, prohibited dependency detected, missing compliance metadata annotation, Golden Path not declared in `service.yaml`.

**First step:** Read the conformance report attached to the ticket. Many failures are genuine configuration gaps that can be fixed without an exception (missing `service.yaml` declaration, outdated dependency version). Fix those first, re-run the pipeline, and close the ticket if the gate passes.
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#exception-type-2-policy-as-code-violation-infrastructure]

### Exception Type 2: Policy-as-Code Violation (Infrastructure)

**Trigger:** The Policy-as-Code Enforcement gate (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002) evaluates a Terraform plan or Kubernetes manifest and produces a hard violation that halts the pipeline.

**Two enforcement modes exist:**
- **Soft warning (`warn`)**: Gate records the violation but does not block the pipeline. No exception required — resolve the warning before the hardening date.
- **Hard violation (`deny`)**: Gate blocks the pipeline. Exception required if the violation cannot be resolved.

Warning-only mode is a **temporary transition state** with a defined hardening date. It is not a permanent configuration, and teams should not treat warnings as non-issues. Every soft warning policy has a documented promotion date to hard violation; the promotion happens on schedule.
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#exception-type-3-verification-contract-check-fitness-function]

### Exception Type 3: Verification Contract Check (Fitness Function)

**Trigger:** A Verification Contract check (PTN-GOV-AI-003) or architecture fitness function (PTN-APP-GOV-001) runs in fail-hard mode and rejects a build.

**Important distinction:** A fitness function failure after a catalog version upgrade (e.g., a new required check introduced in a path minor version) is a migration task, not an exception. Update `context.yaml` to reference the new catalog version and verify the fitness functions pass. Only file an exception if the team genuinely cannot meet the new check requirement.

page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#step-1-triage-by-team--0-to-1-business-day]

### Step 1: Triage (By Team — 0 to 1 Business Day)

When a gate failure generates an exception ticket:

1. Read the attached conformance or policy evaluation report.
2. Determine the violation type. Cross-reference the rule ID against the pattern that owns it:
   - `struct-*` and `dep-*` rule IDs → Architecture Conformance Gate (PTN-INFRA-GOV-001)
   - `ENC-*`, `IAM-*`, `NET-*`, `WARN-*` rule IDs → Policy-as-Code Enforcement (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002)
   - `OBS-*`, `SEC-*`, `META-*` rule IDs → Verification Contract (PTN-GOV-AI-003)
3. Determine whether the violation is a **fixable gap** (missing file, outdated dependency, misconfiguration) or a **genuine technical constraint** (your system legitimately cannot conform to the rule).
4. If fixable: fix it, re-run the pipeline, close the ticket. Do not file an exception for configuration gaps.
5. If a genuine constraint: proceed to Step 2.

**SLA for triage: 1 business day** (PTN-INFRA-GOV-001).
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#step-2-exception-request-submission-by-team]

### Step 2: Exception Request Submission (By Team)

Complete the exception request fields in the ticket:

| Field | What to Write |
|---|---|
| **Business justification** | Why the team cannot conform to the rule. Technical specifics. No marketing language. |
| **Scope** | Which specific repository, service, and rule ID the exception applies to. |
| **Duration** | Proposed duration (maximum 12 months; renewable). |
| **Compensating control** | What you are doing to mitigate the risk the rule is designed to control. Required if one is feasible. |
| **Resolution path** | What would allow the exception to be closed (path change, future migration, path variant). |

**Compensating controls**: A compensating control is a technical or procedural measure that achieves the intent of the rule through an alternative mechanism. For example, a team unable to meet the Kubernetes resource limits policy for a third-party job scheduler might propose running the job in a dedicated namespace with a `ResourceQuota` applied at the namespace level — this achieves resource isolation through namespace-scoped controls rather than per-container limits (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002, Scenario 3). Exceptions with credible compensating controls are more likely to be approved.
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#step-3-arb-review-by-arb--2-week-cycle]

### Step 3: ARB Review (By ARB — 2-Week Cycle)

Exception requests are reviewed by the ARB on their standard 2-week cycle. The ARB may:

- **Approve**: Exception recorded in the Compliance Evidence Store (PTN-GOV-AI-004) with duration and compensating control noted. Pipeline is configured to allow the specific repository to proceed for the exception duration.
- **Approve with conditions**: Additional controls required before approval takes effect. Team addresses conditions and resubmits.
- **Reject**: Exception not approved. Team must resolve the violation. ARB provides specific feedback on the rejection.

> Golden Path exceptions specifically are reviewed on the cadence defined in the Governance Decision Guide in PTN-GOV-AI-001:
>
> | Event | Review Track | Approver | SLA |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Exception to a path requirement | ARB exception review | ARB | 2-week cycle |
> | Security CVE patch (express track) | Express review | CISO sign-off | 48 hours |
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#step-4-exception-in-effect]

### Step 4: Exception in Effect

An approved exception:
- Is recorded in the Compliance Evidence Store with the associated conformance report, business justification, compensating control, and duration.
- Has a defined expiry date. The exception tracker notifies the team 30 days before expiry.
- Does not suppress the violation from reports — violation reports remain visible; the exception record is the audit trail explaining why it was permitted.
page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#step-5-exception-closure]

### Step 5: Exception Closure

Exceptions close in one of three ways:

1. **Path resolution**: The exception prompted a path rule update or new catalog variant that covers the use case. All open exceptions for that rule are closed by Platform Engineering. The exception is the correct signal; not the team's fault.
2. **Team migration**: The team resolves the underlying technical constraint and the violation is remediated. Team closes the exception ticket after the gate passes.
3. **Expiry without renewal**: The exception reaches its duration without resolution. The pipeline returns to fail-hard behavior. This should be avoided — teams should either resolve or renew before expiry.

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#exception-review-decision-guide]

## Exception Review Decision Guide

Use this guide to classify non-conformance before deciding on the exception path:

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| Pipeline fails; I don't know which rule triggered it | Read the conformance or policy evaluation report attached to the auto-created ticket. The rule ID and description are in the report. |
| The failure is a configuration gap (missing file, wrong value) | Fix the gap. Re-run the pipeline. Close the ticket. No exception needed. |
| The failure is triggered by an absolute prohibition | No exception path exists. Redesign to avoid the prohibited action. See PTN-GOV-AI-002 for the prohibition list. |
| The failure is a policy soft warning | No blocking action required yet. Remediate before the hardening date. Check the policy for the promotion schedule. |
| The failure reflects a legitimate technical constraint | Complete the exception request in the ticket. Provide compensating controls. Submit for ARB review. |
| Multiple teams are filing the same exception | This is a path deficiency signal. Raise a catalog improvement ticket alongside the exception. Platform Engineering will evaluate whether a new path variant or rule update is warranted. |
| The path is being deprecated and my service cannot migrate within 90 days | This is a migration timeline issue, not an exception. Contact Platform Engineering through the `#platform-engineering` Slack channel before the deprecation window closes. |
| The exception was approved but the underlying constraint has been resolved | Close the exception ticket. Re-run the pipeline. Confirm the gate now passes. |

---

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#example-1-cronjob-resource-limits-ptn-infra-gov-002]

### Example 1: CronJob Resource Limits (PTN-INFRA-GOV-002)

**Situation:** A new Rego policy (`gainwell.k8s.resource_limits`) was introduced as a soft warning in April 2026, hardening to deny in July 2026. Five of six teams running Kubernetes CronJob workloads remediated within the grace period. One team could not apply per-container resource limits because their CronJob used a third-party job scheduler that sets its own resource configuration internally.

**Exception request:** Team filed an exception with a compensating control: run the scheduler in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace with a `ResourceQuota` enforcing CPU and memory limits at the namespace level, achieving resource isolation through namespace-scoped enforcement.

**Outcome:** Exception approved. The team's compensating control achieved the intent of the rule (prevent unbounded resource usage) through a namespace-level mechanism. The exception surfaced a gap in the ResourceQuota pattern that was added to the infrastructure catalog in the next quarterly review.

**The key:** The team was not trying to avoid the rule. They were asking for a different path to the same outcome.

---
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#example-2-vendor-integration-egress-policy-ptn-gov-ai-001]

### Example 2: Vendor Integration Egress Policy (PTN-GOV-AI-001)

**Situation:** A product team building an integration with a third-party claims platform could not conform to GP-001's egress network policy. The vendor required a non-standard outbound port that the policy did not allow.

**Exception request:** Team submitted a formal exception scoped to the specific service, with a justification documenting the vendor's requirement and no available alternative port.

**Outcome:** The ARB approved a 12-month renewable exception. Platform Engineering was assigned a catalog follow-up item. Six months later, two more teams encountered the same constraint. Platform Engineering published a new catalog variant (`GP-001-EXT-VENDOR-INTEGRATION`) covering the vendor integration pattern. The original exception was marked resolved at its next renewal cycle.

**The key:** The exception was scoped to one service, one rule, and had a time limit. It was also recorded so the statistical signal could be captured — two additional teams hitting the same wall in six months triggered the catalog update.

---
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#example-3-verification-contract--trace-injection-ptn-gov-ai-003]

### Example 3: Verification Contract — Trace Injection (PTN-GOV-AI-003)

**Situation:** GP-001 was bumped to v1.3.0, introducing a new required Verification Contract check (`OBS-003`): trace context must be injected in all outbound HTTP calls. Twelve services migrated within two sprints. Six services opened exception requests: they used a service mesh that handled trace injection transparently at the infrastructure layer, meaning the check would fail even though the capability was present.

**Exception request:** Teams documented the service mesh handling and provided pipeline evidence that traces were being collected correctly at the infrastructure layer.

**Outcome:** Platform Engineering evaluated the exception batch. Rather than approving six individual exceptions, Platform Engineering added a contract exemption for service-mesh-managed trace injection to the Verification Contract v1.3.0. All six exceptions were closed by the platform-level fix.

**The key:** Six exceptions for the same rule in the same path version is a clear signal that the rule needs to account for a legitimate implementation pattern. Exceptions surfaced the gap; the platform fixed it at the source.

---

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#compliance-requirements]

### Compliance Requirements

Approved exceptions and their associated conformance violation records are evidence artifacts. For HIPAA-scoped services, exception records must be retained for a minimum of 6 years (PTN-GOV-AI-004). For FedRAMP-scoped services, 3 years minimum.

An exception approval does not clear the underlying compliance finding from the evidence record. The exception record is the audit trail explanation. Auditors reviewing the evidence store will see both the violation and the approved exception. This is expected and acceptable.

### Monitoring and Metrics

| Metric | Target | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Exception rate (% of deployments with active exceptions) | < 10% per path | Exception tracking registry + conformance gate telemetry |

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#measurement-and-assessment]

## Measurement and Assessment

Exceptions are reviewed at the quarterly catalog review alongside adoption metrics and compliance findings. The review asks:

- Which paths have exception rates > 10%?
- Are multiple teams filing exceptions for the same rule or same path?
- Are exceptions being renewed repeatedly without resolution? (Indicates the path rule may need to change permanently.)
- Have compensating controls been verified as still in effect for multi-year exceptions?

Exception patterns that indicate path deficiencies are escalated to Platform Engineering for catalog update. Exception patterns that indicate team non-compliance (single team, repeated violations, no compensating control) are escalated to the relevant engineering lead.

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-002-exception-management-process.md#tldr]

## TL;DR

```
Gate fails in fail-hard mode → Exception Router creates a ticket automatically.
Read the conformance report → fix if it's a config gap → close the ticket.
If it's a genuine technical constraint → complete the exception request fields → ARB reviews.
Exceptions are scoped, time-limited, and recorded in the evidence store.
Multiple teams filing the same exception = path needs updating, not team discipline.
Absolute prohibition violations (PTN-GOV-AI-002) cannot be excepted — redesign required.
```
